hints: Think about what holds two atoms together in a covalent bond, focusing on the positively charged nuclei and the negatively charged electrons shared between them.
walkthrough:
Picture what is attracting what**
Imagine two nuclei, both positive, both repelling each other. What stops them flying apart? The negative electrons sitting between them. A covalent bond is not just sharing for the sake of it, it is the strong electrostatic pull that the two positive nuclei feel toward that shared negative pair in the middle.
Final answer: A covalent bond is the electrostatic attraction between the nuclei of two atoms and the shared pair of electrons between them.

hints: Count the regions of electron density around each C in C=C, remembering each C forms three sigma bonds and has no lone pairs.
walkthrough:
Link shape to hybridisation**
Look at each carbon in $\text{C=C}$. It joins to three other atoms with sigma bonds and has no lone pairs, so it has three regions of electron density. That gives a trigonal planar arrangement with bond angles of about $120^{\circ}$. In Cambridge language, three regions means $\text{sp}^2$ hybridisation, leaving one unhybridised p orbital on each carbon for the pi bond.
Final answer: Both carbon atoms in C=C are $\text{sp}^2$ hybridised.

hints: Recall the difference in geometry of overlap, head on along the bond axis versus sideways above and below the bond axis.
Think about which orbitals overlap in each case, hybridised orbitals for sigma and unhybridised p orbitals for pi.
walkthrough:
Draw the sigma bond as a head on meeting**
For the $\sigma$ bond, picture two $\text{sp}^2$ hybrid orbitals pointing directly at each other along the line joining the two carbons. They overlap head on, right on the bond axis. Label this as direct overlap. The electron density is concentrated between the two nuclei.

Draw the pi bond as a sideways meeting**
Now leave the $\text{sp}^2$ orbitals alone. Each carbon still has one unhybridised p orbital sticking up and down, parallel to each other. They cannot meet head on, they overlap sideways, forming one lobe of electron density above the $\text{C-C}$ axis and one lobe below it. Label this as sideways overlap of $2 \times$ p orbitals.

Final answer: $\sigma$ bond: diagram showing direct head on overlap of orbitals along the C-C axis between the two C atoms.
$\pi$ bond: diagram showing sideways overlap of two parallel p orbitals, with electron density above and below the C-C axis.

hints: Compare where the electrons sit in a sigma bond versus a pi bond relative to the two nuclei, and what that means for how strongly they are held.
walkthrough:
Compare distance from the nuclei**
In a $\sigma$ bond the electrons sit right between the two nuclei on the bond axis, so both nuclei pull on them strongly. In a $\pi$ bond the electrons sit above and below the axis, further away from the nuclei. Further away means weaker attraction, so less energy is needed to break the $\pi$ bond. That is why an electrophile attacks the exposed $\pi$ electrons and the $\pi$ bond breaks, while the $\sigma$ bond remains.
Final answer: The electron pair in the $\pi$ bond is further from the nuclei than in the $\sigma$ bond, so there is weaker electrostatic attraction and the $\pi$ bond breaks more easily.

hints: Start by identifying the electrophile in H-Br and the nucleophile in the alkene, thinking about bond polarity and the high electron density of C=C.
Consider which carbon of $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C=CH}_2$ gains the H to form the more stable carbocation intermediate.
Recall the structure of 2-methylpropene and work out why addition of H to the $\text{CH}_2$ end gives a tertiary carbocation and the major product.
Think about the final step where the negative bromide ion donates a lone pair to the positively charged carbon.
walkthrough:
Set up the polarity and first attack**
You have $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C=CH}_2$ plus $\text{H-Br}$. Bromine is more electronegative than hydrogen, so label $\text{H}^{\delta+}-\text{Br}^{\delta-}$. The $\text{C=C}$ pi electrons are your nucleophile and $\text{H}^{\delta+}$ is your electrophile. Draw a curly arrow starting at the $\text{C=C}$ double bond and pointing to the $\text{H}$ of $\text{H-Br}$. At the same time draw a second curly arrow from the $\text{H-Br}$ bond onto $\text{Br}$ to make $\text{Br}^-$ with a full lone pair.

Choose the correct carbocation**
The H adds to the carbon that gives the most stable carbocation. If H adds to the $\text{CH}_2$ end, you get $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}^+ - \text{CH}_3$, which is $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}^+$, a tertiary carbocation stabilised by three alkyl groups. If H added the other way you would get only a primary carbocation, much less stable. So draw the tertiary carbocation intermediate with the positive charge on the central carbon.

Finish with bromide attack**
Now $\text{Br}^-$ is a nucleophile with lone pairs. Draw a curly arrow from a lone pair on $\text{Br}^-$ to the $\text{C}^+$ of your tertiary carbocation. This forms the C-Br bond.

Name the major product**
The product is $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CBr}$, which is 2-bromo-2-methylpropane, also called tert-butyl bromide. This is the Markovnikov product because H added to the carbon with more hydrogens and Br ended up on the more substituted carbon.

Final answer: Step 1: $\text{H}^{\delta+}-\text{Br}^{\delta-}$, curly arrow from $\text{C=C}$ to $\text{H}$ of $\text{H-Br}$ and curly arrow from $\text{H-Br}$ bond to $\text{Br}$ to form $\text{Br}^-$ and $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}^+$.
Step 2: lone pair on $\text{Br}^-$ attacks $\text{C}^+$, curly arrow from $\text{Br}^-$ to $\text{C}^+$, to form $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CBr}$, 2-bromo-2-methylpropane as major product.
